cells.tense: What you want and what you do are moving as one.
cells.act: use the finished thing for an hour instead of improving it
cells.ask: Take something you grew that's already done and put it to use for an hour, just as it is. If your hand reaches to fix it, let it rest.
cells.core:
There's something in your care with you right now, and the hours of tending it don't feel like dragging yourself toward a chore. The watering, the checking, the small adjustments all come out of the same motion your heart is in. That's rarer than it sounds. Most people tend a thing while quietly arguing with it.

Going well, this is a person who can finish something and not immediately start the next version. The work gets to land. Nothing here needs correcting. Let a finished thing stay finished for a while instead of turning it into the next project. The next small tending will be there when you get to it.

cells.tense: You will arrive at the outcome before anything has had a chance to grow.
cells.act: bring the two sides of your thinking into one plan
cells.ask: When you catch yourself sketching a thing you tend past its present stage, stop. Bring what you know and what you feel into one line about it, then do only that line.
cells.core:
You've run ahead of what you're growing. The future already has a shape in your head — how it turns out, whether you'll have done it right, how it looks when it's grown — and you keep fitting a seedling to that shape. This isn't neglect. It's care that has turned into managing. The bed stops being a bed and becomes a project with a date on it.

A living thing can't grow toward a picture it wasn't shown. Ease your grip on the picture. Notice when you start sketching the end, and set the sketch aside. The plant will tell you what it needs, in a slower voice than yours. That slower voice is not a problem. It is the one you're supposed to hear.

cells.tense: You were standing at the gate after the season had turned.
cells.act: collect the fruit of the patient wait
cells.ask: Think of a thing you cared for that has already changed or ended, and two things it gave you that are still around. Carry those two around for a few days without doing anything about them.
cells.core:
You've stepped out of the beds. You can still describe what should be planted and when, and you remember the work with your hands, but the present is somewhere you visit rather than live. What's left is the gate and the memory of the work.

This isn't sorrow and it isn't giving up. Something finished, and the finish hasn't landed in you yet, so you keep one foot in the before. But the change did produce something — a quieter week, a freer morning, a thing you know now that you didn't before. Those are real and they're still with you. Turn just far enough to see them, and leave it at that.

cells.tense: The care is happening and you are calling it nothing much.
cells.act: commit to the long build and do today's part
cells.ask: Give today one small piece to whatever you're growing, then stop there. No fixing, no planning the whole thing. Tomorrow, one piece again.
cells.core:
You're tending something faithfully, and the faithfulness has your hands all over it. The right amount of water, the right hour, the right patience — that's craft, and it's been yours for longer than you'd say. You file it under keeping up, or being careful, or that the plant is easy. The plant is easy because you're good at this, and you haven't agreed that your hand is why.

Nobody is asking you to announce anything. Just show up again tomorrow and do the next piece, and notice as you do it that the doing is yours. The plant already knows. You're the last one to find out.

The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you water what you've watered before', so I've cut it to the plain description of what's in the beds.

Too Much's bracing and Too Little's standing-apart are opposite failures of the same capacity: one runs ahead of what's growing, one stays behind it.
